body: Welcome. Over about ninety days you will get one short note a day to help you share your writing, art or ideas with the world, a little at a time.
For now, simply notice the moments you hold back from sharing something. You do not need to change anything yet, just see it.
The fear of being seen is very common among people who make things. It usually means you care about the work, not that the work is bad.
Think of one piece you have made and kept to yourself. Ask what exactly you imagine would happen if someone else saw it.
Most of the harsh critics you picture are inventions of your own mind. Real people tend to scroll past, smile, or quietly enjoy.
Notice the voice that says your work must be perfect before anyone sees it. Perfection is a moving target that keeps you hidden.
Write down three makers whose work you admire. Remember that each of them once shared something for the very first time.
Being seen can feel exposing because your work carries part of you. That tenderness is a sign of honesty, not a reason to hide.
Consider what sharing might give you: connection, feedback, a record of your growth. Hold those gains next to the fear for a moment.
Decide how public you want to be. You can share under your own name, a pen name, or only with a small trusted circle.
Privacy and courage are not opposites. You can keep your face, address or workplace private and still put your work out there.
Notice which kinds of response you fear most. Naming them, even privately in a notebook, makes them a little smaller.
Today, show one finished piece to a single friend you trust. Tell them you are practising sharing, so no detailed critique is needed.
How did it feel to let one person see? Whatever came up, you got through it, and that is real evidence for next time.
A small audience is not a failure. It is where nearly everyone begins, and it is often where the warmest connections are made.
Choose a place online where you could post your work, then look carefully at its privacy settings before sharing anything.
Today, share one small thing publicly: a sketch, a paragraph, a photo of something you made. Then put your phone down and go for a walk.
After posting, the urge to check for reactions can be strong. Try setting a time later in the day when you will look, just once.
Silence after sharing rarely means people disliked it. Most of the time they were busy, or simply have not seen it yet.
Remind yourself why you make things. Write one sentence about it and keep it somewhere you will see before you post.
Numbers measure attention, not worth. A piece seen by five people can still matter deeply to one of them.
Share something unfinished, like a work in progress or a rough idea. Let people see the making, not only the result.
You do not have to explain or apologise for your work when you post it. Let it stand on its own without a list of disclaimers.
Notice if you add phrases like "this is probably rubbish" when sharing. This time, post something without any self put-down.
Leave a kind, specific comment on someone else's creative work. Being generous to other makers helps you feel part of a community.
Consistency matters more than brilliance. A small post every week builds more confidence than one perfect piece a year.
Pick a simple sharing rhythm you could keep, such as once a week. Write it in your diary as a gentle plan, not a strict rule.
If you miss a planned share, you have not failed. Just share the next thing when you are ready, with no catching up needed.
Write a short caption about what inspired your latest piece. A sentence of context helps people connect with what you made.
Feedback is information, not a verdict on you as a person. You get to decide which parts are useful and which to let go.
Think of one piece of criticism you received in the past. Ask whether any part of it helped you, and quietly release the rest.
Some comments are unkind for reasons that have nothing to do with you. You are allowed to delete, block or simply not reply.
Decide in advance how you will respond to a harsh comment. Having a plan makes it far less likely to knock you off balance.
Try sharing a piece somewhere new, perhaps a local group, an email newsletter or a community noticeboard.
Comparing your first steps to someone else's tenth year is unfair to you. Compare yourself only to who you were last month.
Look back at the things you have shared so far. Notice how much braver you have been than you were a month ago.
Ask one person a specific question about your work, such as which part they liked most. Narrow questions invite kind, useful answers.
The urge to delete a post soon after sharing it is common. If it comes today, wait a full day before deciding.
You can be proud of your work and still want to improve it. Both can be true at once without cancelling each other out.
Share something that shows a bit of your personality, not only your polished skill. People connect with people.
Think of a small creator you follow and enjoy. They probably have no idea how much their work means to you, and the same may be true of yours.
Before your next post, check that it does not reveal more than you want, such as your location, routine or full name.
Having boundaries online is part of being a healthy creator. You decide what is shared, when you reply and what stays private.
Experiment with a different format, perhaps a short video, a voice recording or a written thread. Trying new forms keeps sharing light.
Notice what you feel just before you press share. Breathe out slowly, then press anyway, and let the feeling pass on its own.
Share one thing you learnt while making your latest piece. Notes about process often interest people more than you expect.
Not every piece needs to be your best. Some are practice, some are play, and both deserve a place in the world.
Reply warmly to anyone who has commented on your work. Small conversations are how an audience slowly becomes a community.
If a post gets no response at all, that is not a sign to stop. It is simply part of sharing, and it happens to everyone.
Write a short note to your future self about why you keep showing your work, even when things feel quiet.
Set a small limit on how often you check reactions this week. Protecting your attention protects your creativity.
Growth often feels slow from the inside. Looking back over weeks, rather than days, shows the real distance you have travelled.
Share a piece you feel slightly nervous about. A small stretch builds more courage than staying safely comfortable.
You do not need permission to call yourself a writer, artist or thinker. Sharing your work is what makes the title fit.
Say out loud, or write down, "I make things and I share them." Notice how it feels to claim that sentence as yours.
Respond to a shared prompt or join a small group challenge. Making alongside others softens the feeling of being in the spotlight.
Criticism that stings often lands on something you already worry about. Be extra gentle with that tender spot today.
Mute one account that leaves you feeling small. Your feed can support your creative life instead of draining it.
The people who matter most will not care how many likes you get. They will care that you kept going.
Revisit an old piece you never shared. Decide whether to polish it, share it exactly as it is, or let it rest.
You are building a body of work one small share at a time. Over months, these pieces add up to something real.
Tell someone in your offline life about a piece you have shared recently. Let your two worlds meet a little.
It is fine to take breaks from sharing. Rest is part of a creative life, and your work will still be there when you return.
Write a short bio describing what you make. Keep it simple and honest, without shrinking or inflating yourself.
Notice how much less the fear grips you now compared with your first share. It may never vanish, but it has lost some power.
Share something you made purely for fun. Joy is catching, and it reminds people why they love creative work.
Thank one person who encouraged your sharing along the way. Acknowledging encouragement strengthens your circle.
Some days sharing will feel easy and some days it will not. Both are normal, and neither says anything final about you.
Recall one piece of feedback that helped you improve. Notice how being seen has made your work better, not worse.
You are no longer someone who only hides their work. You are someone who shares, even when it feels a bit wobbly.
Jot down loose ideas for your next three shares. A small list makes it easier to keep going on busy days.
Small audiences can be the most loyal. A handful of people who really engage is worth more than a crowd that scrolls by.
Review your privacy settings again. Make sure they still match how visible you want to be now, not how you felt at the start.
Post a piece alongside a short story about the moment the idea came to you. Let people glimpse the person behind it.
When a post does well, enjoy it, then return to your usual rhythm. When it does poorly, do exactly the same.
Notice whether you are making work for yourself or for an imagined audience. Gently steer back towards what you love.
Your work does not need to please everyone. It only needs to find the few people it was meant for.
Encourage someone else who is nervous about sharing. Telling them what helped you will remind you how far you have come.
Being seen gets easier with practice, much like building a muscle. Every small share has been one more repetition.
Share a piece that represents where you are right now, not where you hope to be. Honesty is enough.
You have learnt that silence passes, criticism can be survived and kindness turns up in unexpected places. Hold onto that.
Notice one habit of hiding that has quietly fallen away. Give yourself credit for the change.
Set one gentle creative intention for the coming months, perhaps a project, a series or a new place to share.
The fear may return before a bigger share. When it does, remember you have walked through it many times already.
Read back over your first few shares. Notice the courage in them, whatever you now think of the work itself.
Your voice adds something that no one else can. Keeping it hidden would leave a small gap in the world.
Today, share something and then leave it alone for the rest of the day. Trust the work to do its own job.
You now have a way of sharing that fits you: your pace, your boundaries, your reasons. That is worth protecting.
Write down what sharing your work has given you over these weeks, beyond anything a number could show.
Look back at the person who first opened these notes, nervous about being seen. Notice how much more freely you share now.
Whatever you share next, you know you can handle the silence, the praise and the occasional criticism. You are ready.
Thank you for these ninety days. Keep making, keep sharing in your own way, and let the world see a little more of you.
